understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call a mind that won't settle, and that is where this week begins.
understanding.week_thesis: The restless mind that measures itself against others is the one that will learn to settle, by turning away from the noise and toward what is real.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the restlessness, and the noise that feeds it, named without blame.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that the mind is its own enemy when it runs after the noise of others' success.
week_beats.steady: You hold that what is real in you is not in any comparison, and that is what can settle you.
week_beats.act: You try giving your mind one quiet minute to settle, and bringing it back to what is in front of you.
week_beats.story: A young student who could not settle, running after the noise of a world that seemed ahead, shows you how rest begins.

verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse.sanskrit: चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद्दृढम् । तस्याहं निग्रहं मन्ये वायोरिव सुदुष्करम् ॥
verse.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.
verse.why: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

prasang.title: Mastering the mind
prasang.summary: Arjuna says the mind is restless, stormy and stubborn. Krishna agrees, and says practice and letting go can train it.
prasang.lesson: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

verse.meaning: Arjuna is on the battlefield, and they are telling Krishna that their mind is restless, powerful and stubborn. It feels as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna agrees that the mind is difficult to control, but he says it can be trained through practice and letting go, not by force.
verse.for_you: You are in the middle of studying, and your mind keeps running toward the internships and side startups of others. That restlessness is real, and it is not a flaw.
verse.scene_line: You are on the field, telling your guide that your mind is as hard to hold as the wind.
asks: How can I stop the wind of comparison?
How do I let go when I feel behind?

verse.speaker: Nidagha
verse.sanskrit: इतश्चेतश्च सुव्यग्रं व्यर्थमेवाभिधावति । मनो दूरतरं याति ग्रामे कौलेयको यथा ॥
verse.line: The mind runs here and there for nothing, wandering far like a stray village dog.
verse.translation: The mind runs here and there, restless and pointless; it wanders far away, like a dog in a village.
verse.why: Naming how restless your mind is, is where peace begins.

prasang.title: Nidagha's lament
prasang.summary: Young Nidagha returns from pilgrimage disillusioned and pours out his heart to his teacher Ribhu: life is fleeting, the mind runs like a stray dog, craving gnaws every good quality, and mastering the mind is harder than drinking the ocean.
prasang.lesson: Naming how restless your mind is, is where peace begins.

verse.for_you: While others are building side startups, your own mind runs after their noise like a stray dog. It is not your fault it is restless. You only need to see it clearly.
verse.try_today: Notice when your mind starts chasing someone else's success.
verse.scene_line: Your own mind runs after the noise of others like a stray dog.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: From 'The Way of the Free Ascetic'.
verse.sanskrit: ब्रह्माण्डं मण्डलीमात्रं किं लोभाय मनस्विनः । शफरीस्फुरितेनाब्धिः क्षुब्धो न खलु जायते ॥
verse.line: The ocean is not stirred by a small fish's flick. Petty things needn't shake you.
verse.translation: For the high-minded the whole universe is a mere ring; what is there in it to be greedy for? The ocean is not churned up by the flicker of a little fish.
verse.why: Let others' labels and small things pass; contentment makes you rich.

prasang.title: Vairagyashatakam: The way of the free ascetic
prasang.summary: Portraits of the wandering sage: unbothered when people argue over his caste, sleeping under the sky like a king, and finally bidding farewell to the five elements.
prasang.lesson: Let others' labels and small things pass; contentment makes you rich.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari tells you, the reader, that for someone with a high mind the whole world feels small. He says the ocean does not get stirred up by a little fish flicking its tail. He means that the small movements and labels of others are not worth your disturbance. Let their small actions pass by like a fish in a vast sea. What is real in you is not in any comparison.
verse.for_you: You are in a study room where your friends talk about internships and side startups, and your mind feels small next to their labels. That flicker of comparison is a small fish in the ocean of your own life. The ocean is not stirred by it.
verse.try_today: Notice one small label they use for themselves today.
verse.scene_line: You sit in a study room watching a small fish flicker in the ocean of your own life.
asks: What flickers in the ocean of my own life?
How do I know my ocean is vast enough?

verse.speaker: Ashtavakra
verse.setting: King Janaka asks the young sage Ashtavakra how a person becomes free.
verse.sanskrit: त्वया व्याप्तमिदं विश्वं त्वयि प्रोतं यथार्थतः । शुद्धबुद्धस्वरूपस्त्वं मा गमः क्षुद्रचित्तताम् ॥
verse.line: You are pure awareness, wider than any worry. Don't let your mind shrink into pettiness.
verse.translation: This whole universe is pervaded by you and strung on you. By nature you are pure awareness; do not fall into smallness of mind.
verse.why: You are more than your roles and worries; freedom starts with how you see yourself.

prasang.title: Janaka asks the boy-sage how to be free
prasang.summary: King Janaka, ruler of Mithila, asks the young sage Ashtavakra three questions: how to gain wisdom, freedom and dispassion. Ashtavakra answers at once: you are not the body or your roles but the awareness that watches them, and freedom is available now.
prasang.story_hook: A powerful king bowed before a boy whose body was bent in eight places, and asked him how to be free.
prasang.lesson: You are more than your roles and worries; freedom starts with how you see yourself.

verse.meaning: King Janaka asks the young sage Ashtavakra how to become free. Ashtavakra answers that the whole universe is strung on you, and by nature you are pure awareness. He tells Janaka not to shrink his mind into smallness. This means you are not the restless thoughts or the roles you play. You are the wide awareness that holds them. Freedom is not a prize to win. It is the simple truth of what you are, right now.
verse.for_you: You sit in your room and watch your friends post about internships while your mind races. That comparison is a small fish flicking the ocean of you. You are not that flicker. You are the vast awareness that notices the flicker and then lets it pass.
verse.scene_line: You sit in your room and watch your friends post about internships while your mind races.
asks: How do I see myself when I am not doing anything?
Can I be aware without judging my own thoughts?
What is real in me that no one else can see?

verse.speaker: Rama
verse.setting: After the war, Lakshmana finds Rama alone and asks how to cross the sea of confusion.
verse.sanskrit: विविक्त आसीन उपारतेन्द्रियो विनिर्जितात्मा विमलान्तराशयः । विभावयेदेकमनन्यसाधनो विज्ञानदृक्केवल आत्मसंस्थितः ॥
verse.line: Sit somewhere quiet, let the senses rest, and give your full attention to one thing.
verse.translation: Sitting in a quiet place, senses at rest, self-mastered, pure within, one should contemplate the One with undivided attention, resting in the Self.
verse.why: Quiet sitting and steady faith carry you until understanding becomes natural.

prasang.title: Sit quietly, keep faith
prasang.summary: Rama describes sitting in a quiet place with the senses at rest until the mind becomes like a still ocean, and tells Lakshmana that until he sees the divine everywhere, devotion keeps it alive in the heart.
prasang.lesson: Quiet sitting and steady faith carry you until understanding becomes natural.

verse.meaning: After the war, Lakshmana finds Rama alone and asks how to cross the sea of confusion. Rama tells him to sit somewhere quiet, let the senses rest, and give full attention to one thing. The teaching is that quiet sitting and steady faith carry you until understanding becomes natural. It is not about forcing the mind, but about resting the senses and turning attention to one reality until the storm inside stills.

verse.setting: Vasishtha on effort and grace, after Prahlada's story.
verse.sanskrit: नित्याभ्यासविवेकाभ्यां चित्तमाशु प्रसीदति । आम्र एव दशामेति साहकारीं शनैः शनैः ॥
verse.line: Daily practice and clear thinking make the mind clear, slowly, the way a mango ripens.
verse.translation: Through daily practice and discernment the mind soon becomes clear, just as a mango slowly ripens into its sweetness.
verse.why: Grace and effort work together; keep practising daily, and let the mind ripen slowly.

prasang.title: Prahlada: effort and grace are not rivals
prasang.summary: After telling how Prahlada awakened, Vasishtha faces Rama's challenge: if everything comes by effort, wasn't Prahlada saved by Vishnu's grace? Vasishtha answers that Prahlada earned it himself, that the Self and Vishnu are not two, and that sometimes we wake by our own effort and sometimes by grace reached through devotion. Steady daily practice ripens the mind like a mango.
prasang.lesson: Grace and effort work together; keep practising daily, and let the mind ripen slowly.

verse.meaning: Vasishtha tells Rama that daily practice and clear thinking make the mind clear slowly, the way a mango ripens. He says that through steady effort and discernment the mind becomes sweet in time. Rama had just asked why Prahlada was saved by grace if effort alone matters. Vasishtha answers that grace and effort are not enemies, but partners. The mind ripens when you keep practising, even if the sweetness comes later.
verse.for_you: Your mind is not broken. It is unripe. The comparisons you make are like a green mango, hard and sour, because they come from a place that has not yet ripened. Your family sees the shape of the fruit, but they cannot taste the sweetness you are still growing toward.
verse.try_today: Put the phone down and focus on one task.
verse.scene_line: You are a green mango, still ripening in the quiet sun.
asks: How do I know if I am practising enough?
Can I ripen faster without forcing it?
What is the one task I should focus on?

story.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
story.story_hook: One spring morning, a king out for a walk overheard a song that he could not stop thinking about.
story.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
story.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

anchor.speaker: Janaka
anchor.setting: King Janaka, alone on his palace roof after overhearing wandering sages, rethinks his life.
anchor.sanskrit: संपदश्च विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेच्चित्तेन संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा हन्त मन्ये महापदः ॥ आपदोऽपि विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेन्मनसि संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा मन्ये मनसि संपदः ॥
anchor.line: Good fortune the mind clutches becomes trouble. Trouble the mind accepts becomes a kind of fortune.
anchor.translation: All those dazzling fortunes, if the mind clings to them, are really great calamities in grand disguise. And all those varied misfortunes, if the mind accepts them, are really fortunes.
anchor.why: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.
anchor.misuse: Accepting a hardship doesn't mean not fixing what can be fixed.
